body.text: On October 28, Indonesia’s Presidential Special Envoy for Climate and Energy Hashim Djojohadikusumo announced the country’s target of 7 gigawatts (GW) of nuclear capacity by 2034 as part of the country’s national energy master plan. Indonesia’s push for an aggressive nuclear development strategy reflects its aim to secure domestic energy and power to drive industrialization, especially as it expands as a data center hub and emerges as a semiconductor manufacturing powerhouse.

In pursuit of this goal, Indonesia has been actively seeking foreign expertise to develop its nuclear capabilities, signing agreements with Russia, Singapore, the United States, and Japan earlier this year. These developments highlight the tension that Indonesia currently faces between the quick acquisition of advanced technology from foreign partners and the development of domestic nuclear capacity on its own.

Meeting this demand will require Indonesia to identify sustainable electricity sources to supplement its existing sources of energy. To this end, Indonesia has been pursuing solar projects, wind farms, and other sources of green electricity. However, intermittent renewables by themselves cannot meet this surging demand, and nuclear energy could be vital if Indonesia is to close the ever-increasing gap between its energy demand and the available supply.

To bridge this gap, on October 19, Indonesia signed an agreement with Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom to establish two floating nuclear plants. Leveraging Rosatom’s FPU-100 floating nuclear power units, this initiative is set to provide the northern part of Halmahera Island in North Maluku with a combined 200 MW capacity.

Indonesia’s dispersed island geography provides significant challenges in contrast to nations with connected landmasses, with the Rosatom deal helping to supply reliable electricity to remote coastal regions like in Halmahera Island. However, this agreement is focused around private sector investment, with Rosatom retaining ownership of the floating units and supplying electricity to Indonesian customers.

Therefore, while this agreement does reinforce Indonesia’s domestic energy security initiatives in the short-term, it does little for helping Indonesia develop its long-term energy security initiatives, particularly its goal of establishing a robust nuclear energy sector.

In contrast, a partnership with Japan could offer Indonesia a more viable blueprint for sovereign capacity building. On March 15 of this year, Japan and Indonesia signed a 5-year Memorandum of Cooperation focused on holistic nuclear and energy cooperation. This agreement focused on capacity building, nuclear safety and security, regulatory development, technology selection, and the participation of Japanese companies in Indonesia’s future nuclear program. Furthermore, the bilateral agreement also emphasized the need for a competitive and transparent technology selection process, with this being valuable because it provides Indonesia the flexibility to evaluate reactor technologies that are best positioned to help its own national interests.

Japan is already one of Indonesia’s top five trading partners, with an amended trade agreement between both countries entering into force on August 1, with the goal of strengthening bilateral trade in e-commerce, intellectual property protections, and much more. Japan’s regional proximity to Indonesia and its own expertise in managing a complex, island-based energy grid also make Tokyo a capable partner.
All told, Japan’s cooperation framework offers stark and highly preferable contrast for developing Indonesia’s nuclear ambitions.

Japan has also demonstrated a collaborative approach in working with Indonesia in conjunction with other international partners. In late October, reports emerged that Japan, the U.S., and South Korea were considering exporting jointly-developed nuclear reactors to Indonesia, Malaysia, and the Philippines, under a trilateral cooperation agreement signed earlier in the year. This built upon an announcement in early March 2026, when Indonesia, Japan, and the U.S. hosted a nuclear conference on nuclear small modular reactor deployment in Jakarta.

Furthermore, Japan’s commitment to Indonesian energy sovereignty has extended beyond nuclear power. Last month, Tokyo-based Inpex, Japan’s leading upstream company, took a 50 percent participating interest in BP’s Agung I and Agung II offshore production for natural gas sharing contracts in Indonesia, forming an equal partnership with BP, which will retain the remaining 50 percent and continue as operator.

However, Indonesia does face a variety of structural challenges to establish a robust nuclear industry, whether this be with help from Japan, the United States, or any other country. One of the most significant challenges Indonesia faces is developing a highly technical nuclear-focused workforce. Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency is already investigating this issue alongside agencies like the Ministry of Administrative and Bureaucratic Reform, the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources, the Nuclear Energy Regulatory Agency (Bapeten), and state electricity firm PLN.

However, progress remains limited, with an increase in human resources investments and technical expertise to support the construction and long-term operation of nuclear power plants being desperately needed.

Additionally, Indonesia must ensure that its regulatory framework develops simultaneously alongside its nuclear ambitions. With this in mind, Indonesia has to strengthen its domestic regulatory institutions like Bapeten through international cooperation to develop its own institutional capabilities. The entire nuclear lifecycle requires significant legislation and guardrails, ranging anywhere from preliminary reactor design review to site decommissioning and nuclear waste cleanup.

In both cases, Japan can provide significant value for Indonesia, with Japan’s world-class engineering institutions and culture of rigorous technical training offering immense potential for knowledge transfer. Additionally, in light of lessons learned from the Fukushima nuclear accident, Japan boasts one of the world’s most stringent and battle-tested nuclear regulatory regimes, making it an ideal partner to help Indonesia establish a culture of legislated safety and compliance.

Indonesia’s growing nuclear ambitions can help to secure the country’s domestic energy supply while simultaneously supporting its desire for economic growth. However, the growing gap between Indonesia’s energy consumption and its available supply requires access to nuclear energy. While this need is currently served by foreign partnerships, these partnerships alone will not enable Indonesia to truly secure its energy future. As such, while partnerships with countries like Russia can help immediately address its growing electricity requirements, cooperating with countries like Japan offers Indonesia a better opportunity to establish a robust domestic nuclear industry through capacity building, technological cooperation, and regulatory development instead of simply purchasing nuclear-generated electricity.

As such, Indonesia should evaluate its international nuclear partnerships by the extent to which said partnerships can contribute to the archipelago nation’s long-term technological and industrial development. Therefore, Japan has an opportunity to become an important partner in this process, helping Indonesia move beyond importing nuclear technologies towards the establishment of a nuclear industry that it can independently govern, operate, and sustain.
